To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the productivity of the word pattern is not a significant predictor of the magnitude of word-pattern priming; (2) the productivity of a root is a significant predictor of root priming; (3) the productivity of an unproductive word pattern does not affect root priming; and (4) word-pattern priming does not occur when the word pattern is unproductive.
the productivity of the morpheme is the primary determinant of morphological priming effects in Arabic.

(1) the productivity of the Arabic root is the sole determinant of priming in masked and cross-modal experiments, and (2) this pattern of results is consistent with the idea that the root is the first constituent to be processed when a word is encountered.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between morphological decomposition and productivity in Arabic.
the relationship between productivity and morphemic decomposition in Arabic word recognition.
the relationship between morphological structure and lexical access.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“Arabic is a language that is highly productive in terms of its morphology, and this morphological productivity plays a significant role in its word recognition process” (p. 1).
the Arabic root plays an important role in the on-line decomposition process of Arabic surface forms, and this role is independent of the word pattern.
the root of the Arabic word is the most important factor in the decomposition of the word into morphemic units.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the root is the most important morpheme in Arabic word recognition and that it is the root that is responsible for the morphemic decomposition of the Arabic word.
morphemic decomposition in Arabic is driven by the productivity of morphemes, not the productivity of morphemic classes.
the root, as the semantic core, is the most critical morpheme in the Arabic word, followed by the word pattern, which is the most critical phonological and morphosyntactic marker of wordhood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
morphemic decomposition is not a byproduct of lexical access in Arabic, but is instead a process that is driven by the morphological properties of the input.
Arabic word recognition involves a rapid decomposition of words into their morphemic constituents and that this decomposition is driven by the semantic content of the root.
the productivity of the constituent morphemes of a word is the primary determinant of morphemic decomposition during word recognition.
